nodes.title: Security fundamentals: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Security is about layering defenses so no single failure compromises a system. Most exams test the same core ideas: least privilege, defense in depth, the CIA triad, and the shared-responsibility line between you and your cloud provider.

flashcards.front: What is the CIA triad?
flashcards.back: Confidentiality (only the right people see the data), Integrity (data isn't tampered with), Availability (the system is reachable when needed). Every security control maps to at least one of these three pillars.

flashcards.front: What does 'least privilege' mean?
flashcards.back: Grant each identity (user, role, service account) the minimum permissions needed to do its job — no more. The opposite is wildcard access, which makes a single credential leak catastrophic.

flashcards.front: What is defense in depth?
flashcards.back: Stack multiple, independent controls so an attacker has to defeat all of them. Example: WAF in front of an app, network ACL on the subnet, IAM on the workload, encryption at rest in the database.

flashcards.front: Shared responsibility model — who does what?
flashcards.back: The cloud provider secures the cloud (physical hardware, hypervisor, region facilities). You secure what's IN the cloud (your data, IAM config, OS patching on EC2, application code). The exact line shifts by service: serverless is more on the provider, IaaS is more on you.

pairs.stem: What is the AWS Shared Responsibility Model's 'Security OF the cloud' vs 'IN the cloud'?
pairs.option: Of the cloud: AWS owns hardware, facilities, network. In the cloud: customer owns data, IAM, OS, app security

pairs.stem: What is the AWS Shared Responsibility Model?
pairs.option: AWS secures the cloud (hardware, hypervisor, facilities); customers secure what they put into it

pairs.stem: What is the Principle of Least Privilege in AWS?
pairs.option: Grant administrator permissions broadly so engineers do not hit permission errors at runtime

pairs.stem: What does the 'S' in HTTPS stand for, and which AWS service helps implement it?
pairs.option: Speed — AWS Global Accelerator routes users over the AWS private global backbone

pairs.stem: What is the purpose of AWS CloudTrail?
pairs.option: Deploys and manages cloud infrastructure declaratively with YAML or JSON templates

pairs.stem: What is AWS CloudTrail?
pairs.option: A general-purpose log aggregation service that ingests application logs from any source

nodes.title: Compute services: Key Ideas
nodes.content: 'Compute' is everything that runs your code: VMs, containers, serverless functions, batch jobs. The exam wants you to pick the right shape — long-running stateful workload → VM, packaged app → container, event-driven short job → serverless.

flashcards.front: VM vs container vs serverless — pick a service for each.
flashcards.back: VM (EC2 / Compute Engine / Azure VM) when you need full OS control. Container (ECS, GKE, AKS, Cloud Run) when you've packaged an app and want orchestration. Serverless (Lambda, Functions, Cloud Functions) for short event-driven tasks, no infrastructure to manage.

flashcards.front: What is autoscaling?
flashcards.back: A service that adds/removes compute instances based on a signal (CPU, request rate, queue depth, custom metric). Scale-out is cheap; scale-in saves money. Target tracking is the simplest mode: 'keep average CPU at 60%'.

flashcards.front: Spot / preemptible / low-priority — what's the catch?
flashcards.back: Up to 90% off list price, but the cloud can yank the instance with 30 s – 2 min warning. Use for fault-tolerant batch jobs, CI runners, big-data clusters. Don't use for stateful databases or anything that needs to stay up.

flashcards.front: Reserved / committed-use vs on-demand pricing.
flashcards.back: On-demand: pay by the hour or second, no commitment. Reserved / committed: 1-3 year commitment, 30-60% discount, no flexibility. Pick reserved for steady baseline load, on-demand for spiky workloads.

pairs.stem: What is AWS Elastic Load Balancing?
pairs.option: Distributes incoming traffic across EC2, container, IP, and Lambda targets for availability

pairs.stem: Which AWS service provides serverless container execution?
pairs.option: Amazon EKS managed Kubernetes control plane

pairs.stem: What is AWS Elastic Beanstalk?
pairs.option: An infrastructure-as-code tool that synthesizes templates from imperative code

pairs.stem: What is AWS Auto Scaling?
pairs.option: Automatically adjusts compute capacity by adding or removing instances based on demand

pairs.stem: Which AWS service allows you to run code without provisioning servers?
pairs.option: AWS Lambda

pairs.stem: What is the difference between horizontal and vertical scaling?
pairs.option: Horizontal scaling applies to relational databases; vertical applies to compute fleets

nodes.title: Storage concepts: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Cloud storage comes in three flavors with very different cost/perf trade-offs: object (think S3), block (think EBS / managed disks), and file (think EFS / Azure Files / Filestore). Pick wrong and you either overpay or hit performance ceilings.

flashcards.front: Object vs block vs file storage — when do you use each?
flashcards.back: Object (S3, Blob, GCS) for unstructured data, backups, static sites, data lakes — flat namespace, HTTP API, infinite scale. Block (EBS, managed disks) for OS disks and databases — low latency, single attach. File (EFS, NFS) when multiple VMs need a shared POSIX filesystem.

flashcards.front: What is a storage class / tier?
flashcards.back: Same data, different SLA and price. Hot tier (frequent access, expensive read, cheap retrieval). Cold/archive tier (rare access, cheap to store, expensive to read, retrieval latency from minutes to hours). Lifecycle policies move data between tiers automatically.

flashcards.front: Why use server-side encryption?
flashcards.back: Data is encrypted at rest by the storage service using either provider-managed keys (default, no extra config) or your own keys via KMS. This protects against physical disk theft and meets compliance baselines without changing your app code.

flashcards.front: What's storage durability vs availability?
flashcards.back: Durability is the chance your data won't be lost (object stores claim ~11 9s — 99.999999999%). Availability is the chance you can reach it right now (typically 4 9s — 99.99%). Durability is multi-region replication; availability is how many concurrent failures the service tolerates.

pairs.stem: What is Amazon EFS?
pairs.option: An elastic NFS file system that multiple EC2 instances can mount simultaneously

pairs.stem: What is AWS Snowball?
pairs.option: A CloudFront edge location that caches content close to end users

pairs.stem: What is Amazon FSx?
pairs.option: Managed file systems including FSx for Windows, Lustre, NetApp ONTAP, and OpenZFS

pairs.stem: Which AWS service provides scalable object storage?
pairs.option: Amazon S3

pairs.stem: What is Amazon EBS?
pairs.option: Persistent block storage volumes for EC2 that outlive the instance and can be reattached

pairs.stem: What is AWS DataSync?
pairs.option: A managed database synchronization service that replicates RDS data across Regions

nodes.title: Identity and access management: Key Ideas
nodes.content: IAM is the layer that decides who can do what. It's almost always the first thing to misconfigure and the most common security failure mode. Every cloud uses the same primitives — identities, policies, roles — under slightly different names.

flashcards.front: What's the difference between authentication and authorization?
flashcards.back: Authentication (AuthN) proves who you are — password, MFA, certificate. Authorization (AuthZ) decides what you're allowed to do once authenticated — policies, roles, ACLs. AuthN happens first; AuthZ is checked on every request.

flashcards.front: What is a role (vs a user)?
flashcards.back: A user is a long-lived identity tied to a person. A role is a short-lived, assumable identity — services or users 'become' the role to get temporary credentials. Roles let you grant access without sharing long-term keys. Always prefer roles.

flashcards.front: Identity-based vs resource-based policies.
flashcards.back: Identity-based policies attach to a user / role and say what THEY can do. Resource-based policies attach to a thing (S3 bucket, KMS key, SQS queue) and say who can access IT. Cross-account access usually needs both: target's resource policy says 'allow this account', source identity policy says 'allow this action on that resource'.

flashcards.front: Why federation / SSO?
flashcards.back: Instead of creating cloud users for every employee, federate from your corporate identity provider (Okta, Azure AD, Google Workspace). Users sign in once with their work account; the IdP issues a SAML / OIDC token; the cloud trades it for temporary credentials. One source of truth, instant deprovisioning.

pairs.stem: What is the principle of least privilege in AWS IAM?
pairs.option: Grant users the minimum permissions required to perform their assigned tasks

pairs.stem: A developer needs to give an EC2 instance permission to read from one specific S3 bucket. Following AWS best practice, which approach should they use?
pairs.option: Identity and Access Management — who can do what in AWS

pairs.stem: What is an IAM Policy Evaluation — what happens when Allow and Deny exist?
pairs.option: Evaluation depends on the order in which IAM policies were attached to the principal

pairs.stem: What is the difference between AWS Managed Policies and Customer Managed Policies?
pairs.option: AWS Managed Policies and Customer Managed Policies behave identically at evaluation time

pairs.stem: What is AWS IAM Role?
pairs.option: An assumable IAM identity with permissions and short-lived credentials via STS

pairs.stem: What is IAM Access Analyzer?
pairs.option: A cost analysis tool that attributes spend to resources, accounts, tags, and services

nodes.title: Cloud billing and cost: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Cloud cost optimization is mostly visibility + commitments. You can't optimize what you can't see, and you can't commit without forecasts. Most exams test the savings instruments (reserved instances, savings plans, sustained use) and the visibility tools.

flashcards.front: Where do you see cloud spend?
flashcards.back: AWS Cost Explorer / Azure Cost Management / GCP Billing reports. Filter by tag, service, account, region. Set up budget alerts (notify when 80% / 100% of monthly budget is hit) so a runaway autoscaler doesn't surprise you on the 28th.

flashcards.front: Reserved Instance vs Savings Plan vs Spot — pick the right one.
flashcards.back: RI / committed-use: 1-3 yr commitment, 30-60% off, locked to instance family/region. Savings Plan: 1-3 yr commitment on $/hr spend, more flexible across instance types. Spot/preemptible: up to 90% off, can be reclaimed any moment. Use commitments for steady baseline, spot for fault-tolerant workloads.

flashcards.front: What's the egress (data transfer out) cost trap?
flashcards.back: Most clouds charge nothing to ingest data but $0.05-$0.12/GB to send it OUT. Inter-region replication, public-facing APIs, multi-cloud data movement — all add up fast. Mitigations: same-region peering, CloudFront / CDN caching, VPC endpoints to keep traffic on the AWS backbone.

flashcards.front: What is a unit cost / cost per X?
flashcards.back: Cost-per-request, cost-per-active-user, cost-per-transaction. Total cloud spend is a vanity metric — engineers can't act on '$50k/month'. Unit cost ($0.003 per request) reveals whether you got cheaper or more expensive as you scaled, which is what optimization actually means.

pairs.stem: What is the AWS Free Tier?
pairs.option: Limited free usage for 12 months on new accounts plus always-free and short trial offers

pairs.stem: What is the AWS Pricing Calculator?
pairs.option: A monthly cost savings report comparing actual spend to a defined budget baseline

pairs.stem: What is AWS Organizations?
pairs.option: A managed directory of IAM users with built-in single sign-on for the AWS Console

pairs.stem: What is AWS Cost Explorer?
pairs.option: A tool to visualize and analyze actual AWS cost and usage with granular filtering

pairs.stem: What is AWS Budgets?
pairs.option: A cost analysis tool that visualizes historical spend trends across services and tags

pairs.stem: Which tool helps estimate monthly AWS costs before deploying resources?
pairs.option: AWS Pricing Calculator

nodes.title: Mixed Topics: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Quick primer on Mixed Topics. Tap to flip cards covering the most-asked exam ideas in this domain.

flashcards.front: What is the purpose of an Internet Gateway in a VPC?
flashcards.back: An Internet Gateway (IGW) is a horizontally-scaled, redundant VPC component that enables communication between VPC instances and the internet.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between a Security Group and a Network ACL?
flashcards.back: SG: stateful (return traffic auto-allowed), instance level, allow rules only, evaluated as a whole. NACL: stateless (return traffic needs explicit rule), subnet level, ordered allow/deny rules. instance-level, allow-only rules. Network ACLs: stateless, subnet-level, allow AND deny rules

flashcards.front: What is the purpose of an AWS NAT Gateway?
flashcards.back: A NAT Gateway in a public subnet allows private subnet instances to reach the internet for updates/patches while remaining unreachable from inbound internet connections.

flashcards.front: What is VPC Peering vs Transit Gateway?
flashcards.back: VPC Peering: simple, low-cost, no transitive routing (A↔B and B↔C doesn't mean A↔C). Transit Gateway: scalable hub for 1000s of VPCs and VPNs with transitive routing, route tables, and multicast support.

pairs.stem: What is the purpose of an Internet Gateway in a VPC?
pairs.option: Provides outbound and inbound internet access for resources in public subnets

pairs.stem: What is Amazon CloudFront?
pairs.option: A global CDN with hundreds of edge locations caching content close to end users

pairs.stem: What is an EC2 Security Group?
pairs.option: A VPC route table entry that forwards specific destination CIDRs to a target gateway

pairs.stem: What is an AWS Availability Zone (AZ)?
pairs.option: A globally distributed CloudFront edge location that caches content close to end users

pairs.stem: What is an AMI (Amazon Machine Image)?
pairs.option: A template containing OS, applications, and configuration used to launch EC2 instances

pairs.stem: What is Amazon Route 53?
pairs.option: A scalable DNS and domain registration service with routing policies
